Eigenvectors and eigenvalues, for programmers

The common piece behind PCA, Markov chains, the Kalman filter and the speed of gradient descent: definition and characteristic polynomial, diagonalization and powers, the spectral theorem and the Rayleigh quotient, how they are really computed (power, inverse iteration, QR, LAPACK), Perron–Frobenius and mixing speed, and the condition number of a Hessian. With a from-scratch module verified against NumPy and scikit-learn, a simulated fleet and a worked example by hand.

Summary

  • The eigenvalues of are the roots of . In 2 × 2: , with trace and determinant . They can be complex (rotations).
  • If there are independent eigenvectors, and : the long-run behavior is decided by . A shear is not diagonalizable.
  • Symmetric: with orthogonal and real; .
  • The power method converges like ; shifted inverse iteration, like . In production: shifted QR (LAPACK, eig/eigh) or Lanczos/Arnoldi for large sparse matrices.
  • Markov: the stationary distribution is the eigenvector of with ; sets the mixing speed. PCA: eigenvectors of the covariance. Gradient descent: its speed depends on the Hessian's .
Av = λv→ det(A − λI) = 0→ A = VΛV⁻¹→ symmetric: QΛQᵀ→ power, QR→ Markov, PCA, GD

§1 · Definition

Invariant directions and the characteristic polynomial

An eigenvector of is a whose image is parallel to it, ; is its eigenvalue. With the reading from topic 3 (a matrix is a linear transformation), it is a line through the origin that the transformation leaves invariant, stretched by . has a nonzero solution if and only if is singular:

A real polynomial of degree has complex roots counting multiplicity; the complex ones come in conjugate pairs. The set of eigenvectors of (plus zero) is the subspace : eigenvectors have no length or sign of their own, and libraries return a unit one with an arbitrary sign. In 2 × 2, with and :

(the one with the larger norm is used; if both are zero, and every vector is an eigenvector). With a negative discriminant there are no real invariant directions. The typical case is a rotation by angle scaled by :

The modulus still has meaning: each application scales by while rotating by , and the complex eigenvectors describe the plane in which it rotates. Every real 2 × 2 with complex eigenvalues is similar to one of these. Multiplicities. The algebraic one is that of the root; the geometric one, , and it can be smaller: the shear has a double but a single eigendirection (§2).

The trace–determinant plane. The two numbers decide everything in 2 × 2: above the parabola the eigenvalues are complex; below it, real; with , real with opposite signs. For a system that repeats itself, , both satisfy exactly inside the triangle (Jury criterion). The α–β filter of idea 5 of the simple version has error matrix , with and : the triangle turns into the classic region .

§2 · Diagonalization

Powers, modes and matrices that won't cooperate

If has linearly independent eigenvectors (for example, if its eigenvalues are distinct), they are stacked as the columns of and :

In the eigenvector basis, is diagonal: each coordinate evolves on its own. If (),

Each term is a mode: it grows if , fades if , alternates sign if and rotates if it is complex. In the long run the one with the largest modulus dominates, and the spectral radius decides the stability of : if and only if (this also holds without diagonalizing). Matrix functions are defined the same way: solves , stable if .

When it can't be done. The shear has a double and only the eigenvector . It is not diagonalizable, and

grows linearly even though . In general, the Jordan form adds blocks with ones above the diagonal and terms . Numerically the Jordan form is unstable (a perturbation of splits the double eigenvalue into ), so in practice the Schur form is used, with unitary and triangular; it always exists and it is what the QR algorithm computes.

Sensitivity. If is diagonalizable and is perturbed by , each eigenvalue of is within of some eigenvalue of (Bauer–Fike). With an ill-conditioned (nearly parallel eigenvectors, strongly non-symmetric matrices), the eigenvalues are fragile, and moreover can grow a lot before decaying even though . For symmetric matrices and none of this happens.

§3 · Symmetric matrices

Spectral theorem, quadratic forms and the Rayleigh quotient

Spectral theorem. If , its eigenvalues are real and there is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors:

The two key pieces fit in one line. Real: if with , is real. Orthogonal: if , forces . Geometrically: every symmetric matrix is “rotate to the eigen-axes, stretch each axis, undo the rotation”. Covariances, Hessians, kernels, graph Laplacians and are symmetric, and that's why this case dominates ML.

Quadratic forms. In the eigenbasis, ,

is positive definite () if and only if all ; the level curves are ellipses with semi-axes along the directions . With , they are the ellipses of a Gaussian (Mahalanobis distance). Rayleigh quotient:

The last line is Courant–Fischer: each eigenvalue is an optimization problem. It is what turns “the direction of maximum variance” (PCA, §6) into “the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue of the covariance”. Moreover, is stationary at the eigenvectors: if with , : a vector with 6 correct digits gives an eigenvalue with about 12. You'll see it in §7.

Locating without computing. Gershgorin: every eigenvalue lies in some disk . For a row-stochastic matrix, all the disks lie inside the unit disk: (§5).

§4 · How they are computed

Power method, inverse iteration and QR

Above there is no formula in radicals for the roots (Abel–Ruffini), and even if there were, computing the characteristic polynomial and its roots is numerically disastrous. All methods are iterative. Power method: . By §2, if and ,

It only needs products : it works for huge sparse matrices that are never even stored whole (PageRank). Its weak spot is the ratio: with , ten digits cost about 2,300 iterations. Shifted inverse iteration: the power method on , whose eigenvalues are ; it converges to the eigenvalue closest to with ratio

is factored once (LU) and each iteration is a substitution. If is updated with the Rayleigh quotient at each step (Rayleigh quotient iteration), convergence is cubic for symmetric matrices. conv.py measures it with a 50 × 50 symmetric matrix and random eigenvectors:

conv.py

import numpy as np
from autovectores import potencia, potencia_inversa

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(50, 50)))             # eigenvectors: a random orthonormal basis of R⁵⁰
print("|λ₂/λ₁|  iterations until direction error < 1e-10      prediction log(1e-10)/log|λ₂/λ₁|")
for r in [0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99]:
    S = Q @ np.diag(np.r_[10.0, 10 * r, rng.uniform(0, 9 * r, 48)]) @ Q.T
    x = rng.normal(size=50); x /= np.linalg.norm(x); v1 = Q[:, 0]; it = 0
    while min(np.linalg.norm(x - v1), np.linalg.norm(x + v1)) > 1e-10:
        x = S @ x; x /= np.linalg.norm(x); it += 1
    print(f"{r:6.2f}   {it:8d}                                       {np.log(1e-10) / np.log(r):8.0f}")
# λ₁ = 10, λ₂ = 9.9: the power method struggles; shifted inverse iteration converges to the eigenvalue closest to μ
S = Q @ np.diag(np.r_[10.0, 9.9, rng.uniform(0, 8, 48)]) @ Q.T
l, v, k = potencia(S, rng.normal(size=50), tol=1e-14, max_iter=100_000)
print(f"power:               λ = {l:.12f}  in {k} iterations")
for mu in [9.0, 9.97, 10.01]:
    l, v, k = potencia_inversa(S, mu, x0=rng.normal(size=50), tol=1e-14)
    print(f"inverse, μ = {mu:5.2f}:  λ = {l:.12f}  in {k:3d} iterations   (ratio |λ₁−μ|/|λ₂−μ| = {abs(10 - mu) / abs(9.9 - mu):.3f})")

actual output

# |λ₂/λ₁|  iterations until direction error < 1e-10      prediction log(1e-10)/log|λ₂/λ₁|
#   0.10         11                                             10
#   0.50         32                                             33
#   0.90        218                                            219
#   0.99       2409                                           2291
# power:               λ = 9.999999999995  in 1569 iterations
# inverse, μ =  9.00:  λ = 9.900000000000  in 116 iterations   (ratio |λ₁−μ|/|λ₂−μ| = 1.111)
# inverse, μ =  9.97:  λ = 10.000000000000  in  19 iterations   (ratio |λ₁−μ|/|λ₂−μ| = 0.429)
# inverse, μ = 10.01:  λ = 10.000000000000  in   8 iterations   (ratio |λ₁−μ|/|λ₂−μ| = 0.091)

The prediction is right up to a constant (it depends on , that is, on the starting vector). With and , the power method takes 1,569 iterations; with inverse iteration needs 8. And with it converges... to 9.9, which is the closest to : inverse iteration finds the eigenvalue you ask for, not the largest one.

The QR algorithm (Francis, 1961; Kublanovskaya, 1961) is what libraries use for dense matrices. It factors and forms : a similarity, which preserves eigenvalues. It is equivalent to running the power method on all vectors at once (with orthogonalization) and, with shifts, inverse iteration on the last one; the last row converges to and is deflated. First is reduced to Hessenberg form (tridiagonal if symmetric) in , so that each step costs (or ). In total, about flops for all eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a non-symmetric matrix, quite a bit fewer for a symmetric one.

§5 · Markov chains

Stationary distribution, Perron–Frobenius and mixing speed

With (rows that add up to 1) and the distribution as a row vector, . A stationary distribution satisfies

It is a left eigenvector of with eigenvalue 1. That eigenvalue always exists: , and , share the characteristic polynomial. By Gershgorin (§3), no eigenvalue has modulus greater than 1. Perron–Frobenius: if the chain is irreducible (every state can reach every state) and aperiodic, eigenvalue 1 is simple, its eigenvector has all positive entries, and all the others satisfy . Then, wherever it starts,

The spectral gap sets the speed: the mixing time (steps until total variation distance from the worst start) is of the order of for reversible chains. In 2 × 2, with : and . If the chain is periodic (a truck that alternates road and rest every day), appears and the distribution oscillates without converging; if it is reducible, there are several stationary distributions.

Computing it: the power method on (products only, ideal for large sparse chains like PageRank, which adds a random jump to guarantee Perron–Frobenius), or a linear system with one equation replaced by . The rest of the theory (estimating , hitting times, hidden models) is in the technical version of Markov chains.

§6 · PCA and gradient descent

The shape of the data and the shape of the valley

PCA. With centered (), the sample covariance is symmetric positive semidefinite. The variance of the projection onto a unit vector is , so by §3 the direction of maximum variance is the eigenvector of , the next one (orthogonal) that of , and so on:

In practice it is computed with the SVD of (), without forming (which squares the condition number, as in topic 4): that's what scikit-learn does and it is topic 6. The details of PCA (reconstruction, Eckart–Young, scaling, how many components) are in the technical version of PCA.

Gradient descent. Near a minimum, the loss is approximately quadratic with Hessian : . With a fixed step , the error evolves like a linear system:

The step is limited by the most curved direction (); progress, by the flattest one (). With a large the valley is a ditch: the gradient points almost at the wall, the iterate bounces between the two walls (zigzag, eigenvalue close to −1) and crawls along the bottom at a snail's pace. Polyak's momentum lowers the factor to ; standardizing the features (topic 7 of Preparing the data) reduces directly. More in the technical version of gradient descent.

gd.py

import numpy as np
# f(w) = ½ wᵀHw with H = diag(λmax, λmin): gradient descent w ← w − η H w with the best fixed step η = 2/(λmax+λmin)
print(" κ = λmax/λmin   factor per step (κ−1)/(κ+1)   steps until ‖w‖ < 1e-6‖w₀‖   with momentum (heavy ball)")
for kappa in [1, 10, 100, 1000]:
    H = np.diag([float(kappa), 1.0]); eta = 2 / (kappa + 1)
    w = np.array([1.0, 1.0]); k = 0
    while np.linalg.norm(w) > 1e-6 * np.sqrt(2): w = w - eta * H @ w; k += 1
    # Polyak: η = 4/(√L+√μ)², β = ((√κ−1)/(√κ+1))²
    eta2 = 4 / (np.sqrt(kappa) + 1) ** 2; beta = ((np.sqrt(kappa) - 1) / (np.sqrt(kappa) + 1)) ** 2
    w = np.array([1.0, 1.0]); wp = w.copy(); j = 0
    while np.linalg.norm(w) > 1e-6 * np.sqrt(2) and j < 10**6: w, wp = w - eta2 * H @ w + beta * (w - wp), w; j += 1
    print(f"{kappa:8d}          {(kappa - 1) / (kappa + 1):.4f}                     {k:6d}                        {j:5d}")

actual output

#  κ = λmax/λmin   factor per step (κ−1)/(κ+1)   steps until ‖w‖ < 1e-6‖w₀‖   with momentum (heavy ball)
#        1          0.0000                          1                            1
#       10          0.8182                         69                           27
#      100          0.9802                        691                           93
#     1000          0.9980                       6908                          315

The number of steps grows linearly with (about ) and, with momentum, with . For one step is enough: with and all curvatures equal, the gradient points at the minimum.

§7 · From scratch

Power, inverse, deflation, Jacobi, QR, Markov and PCA, verified

autovectores.py

"""Eigenvalues and eigenvectors from scratch: closed-form 2×2, power, shifted inverse, deflation, Jacobi, QR, Markov and PCA."""
import numpy as np

def eig2(A):
    """Eigenvalues of a 2×2 via trace and determinant: λ = t/2 ± √(t²/4 − d). Complex if the discriminant is < 0."""
    t = A[0, 0] + A[1, 1]; d = A[0, 0] * A[1, 1] - A[0, 1] * A[1, 0]
    disc = t * t / 4 - d
    r = np.sqrt(complex(disc)) if disc < 0 else np.sqrt(disc)
    return np.array([t / 2 + r, t / 2 - r])

def potencia(A, x0=None, tol=1e-12, max_iter=10_000):
    """Power method: x ← Ax/‖Ax‖. Returns (dominant λ, unit eigenvector, iterations).
    Converges if |λ₁| > |λ₂|, with direction error ~ |λ₂/λ₁|^k."""
    A = np.asarray(A, float); n = A.shape[0]
    x = np.ones(n) / np.sqrt(n) if x0 is None else np.asarray(x0, float) / np.linalg.norm(x0)
    lam = 0.0
    for k in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        y = A @ x
        lam_nuevo = x @ y                       # Rayleigh quotient (x is a unit vector)
        x_nuevo = y / np.linalg.norm(y)
        if x_nuevo @ x < 0:                     # negative λ: the vector flips direction at every step
            x_nuevo = -x_nuevo
        if abs(lam_nuevo - lam) <= tol * abs(lam_nuevo) and np.linalg.norm(x_nuevo - x) < np.sqrt(tol):
            return lam_nuevo, x_nuevo, k
        x, lam = x_nuevo, lam_nuevo
    return lam, x, max_iter

def potencia_inversa(A, mu, x0=None, tol=1e-12, max_iter=500):
    """Shifted inverse iteration: power method on (A − μI)⁻¹. Finds the eigenvalue closest to μ.
    It is factored once (here with solve at each step so as not to depend on scipy)."""
    A = np.asarray(A, float); n = A.shape[0]; B = A - mu * np.eye(n)
    x = np.ones(n) / np.sqrt(n) if x0 is None else np.asarray(x0, float) / np.linalg.norm(x0)
    lam = mu
    for k in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        y = np.linalg.solve(B, x); x_nuevo = y / np.linalg.norm(y)
        lam_nuevo = x_nuevo @ A @ x_nuevo
        if abs(lam_nuevo - lam) <= tol * max(1.0, abs(lam_nuevo)):
            return lam_nuevo, x_nuevo, k
        x, lam = x_nuevo, lam_nuevo
    return lam, x, max_iter

def deflacion(S, k=None, tol=1e-13):
    """Eigenpairs of a symmetric matrix: power method + Hotelling deflation S ← S − λ v vᵀ.
    Sorted by |λ| (what the power method finds). Didactic: the error accumulates from one pair to the next."""
    S = np.array(S, float); n = S.shape[0]; k = n if k is None else k
    vals, vecs = [], []
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    for _ in range(k):
        lam, v, _ = potencia(S, rng.normal(size=n), tol=tol)
        vals.append(lam); vecs.append(v)
        S = S - lam * np.outer(v, v)
    return np.array(vals), np.array(vecs).T

def jacobi(S, tol=1e-14, max_barridos=50):
    """Cyclic Jacobi for symmetric matrices: Givens rotations that zero out each a_pq. Returns (λ, V) with S = V diag(λ) Vᵀ."""
    A = np.array(S, float); n = A.shape[0]; V = np.eye(n)
    for _ in range(max_barridos):
        off = np.sqrt(np.sum(np.tril(A, -1) ** 2))
        if off < tol * np.linalg.norm(A):
            break
        for p in range(n - 1):
            for q in range(p + 1, n):
                if abs(A[p, q]) < 1e-300:
                    continue
                theta = (A[q, q] - A[p, p]) / (2 * A[p, q])
                t = np.sign(theta) / (abs(theta) + np.sqrt(theta * theta + 1)) if theta != 0 else 1.0
                c = 1 / np.sqrt(t * t + 1); s = t * c
                G = np.eye(n); G[p, p] = G[q, q] = c; G[p, q] = s; G[q, p] = -s
                A = G.T @ A @ G; V = V @ G          # O(n³) per rotation: clear, not efficient
    lam = np.diag(A).copy(); idx = np.argsort(lam)[::-1]
    return lam[idx], V[:, idx]

def qr_simetrica(S, tol=1e-13, max_iter=10_000):
    """QR iteration with Wilkinson shift and deflation, for small symmetric matrices.
    A ← RQ + μI preserves the eigenvalues (it is Qᵀ(A−μI)Q + μI) and pushes the last row to (0, …, 0, λ)."""
    A = np.array(S, float); n = A.shape[0]; V = np.eye(n); m = n; it = 0
    while m > 1 and it < max_iter:
        it += 1
        a, b, c = A[m - 2, m - 2], A[m - 2, m - 1], A[m - 1, m - 1]
        d = (a - c) / 2; sg = 1.0 if d >= 0 else -1.0
        mu = c - sg * b * b / (abs(d) + np.hypot(d, b)) if b != 0 else c   # eigenvalue of the trailing 2×2 closest to c
        Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A[:m, :m] - mu * np.eye(m))
        A[:m, :m] = R @ Q + mu * np.eye(m)
        A[:m, m:] = Q.T @ A[:m, m:]; A[m:, :m] = A[:m, m:].T
        V[:, :m] = V[:, :m] @ Q
        if abs(A[m - 1, m - 2]) < tol * (abs(A[m - 1, m - 1]) + abs(A[m - 2, m - 2])):
            m -= 1
    lam = np.diag(A).copy(); idx = np.argsort(lam)[::-1]
    return lam[idx], V[:, idx], it

def estacionaria(P, metodo="potencia", tol=1e-14, max_iter=100_000):
    """Stationary distribution of a Markov chain (P by rows: P[i, j] = Pr(i → j)).
    π is a left eigenvector with λ = 1: πP = π, Σπ = 1."""
    P = np.asarray(P, float); n = P.shape[0]
    if metodo == "lineal":                       # (Pᵀ − I)π = 0 with one equation replaced by Σπ = 1
        M = P.T - np.eye(n); M[-1, :] = 1.0
        b = np.zeros(n); b[-1] = 1.0
        return np.linalg.solve(M, b)
    pi = np.ones(n) / n
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        nuevo = pi @ P
        if np.abs(nuevo - pi).sum() < tol:
            return nuevo / nuevo.sum()
        pi = nuevo
    return pi / pi.sum()

def tiempo_mezcla(P, eps=0.01):
    """Steps until, wherever it starts, the distribution is within total variation distance < eps of π."""
    P = np.asarray(P, float); pi = estacionaria(P, "lineal"); Pk = np.eye(len(P))
    for k in range(1, 100_000):
        Pk = Pk @ P
        if 0.5 * np.abs(Pk - pi).sum(axis=1).max() < eps:
            return k
    return None

def pca(X, k=None):
    """PCA via eigenvectors of the (symmetric) covariance: Jacobi. Returns (components as rows, variances, mean).
    Sign fixed so that the largest entry of each vector is positive (eigenvectors have no sign of their own)."""
    X = np.asarray(X, float); mu = X.mean(0); Xc = X - mu
    C = Xc.T @ Xc / (len(X) - 1)
    lam, V = jacobi(C)
    k = len(lam) if k is None else k
    V = V[:, :k] * np.sign(V[np.argmax(np.abs(V[:, :k]), axis=0), np.arange(k)])
    return V.T, lam[:k], mu

check.py

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from autovectores import (eig2, potencia, potencia_inversa, deflacion, jacobi, qr_simetrica,
                          estacionaria, pca)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def simetrica_separada(n):
    """Random symmetric matrix with well-separated eigenvalues (distinct |λ|), so that the power method converges."""
    Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(n, n)))
    lam = rng.permutation(np.r_[rng.uniform(1, 10, n // 2 + n % 2), -rng.uniform(0.5, 9.5, n // 2)])
    lam = np.sign(lam) * (np.abs(lam) + 0.15 * np.arange(n)[np.argsort(np.argsort(np.abs(lam)))])
    return Q @ np.diag(lam) @ Q.T
def mismo_vector(u, v):
    """Distance between directions: eigenvectors are only defined up to sign."""
    return min(np.linalg.norm(u - v), np.linalg.norm(u + v))

e = dict.fromkeys(["eig2", "pot", "potv", "inv", "def", "jac", "jacv", "qr", "qrv", "rec", "est", "pca", "pcav", "evr"], 0.0)
for _ in range(300):
    A = rng.normal(size=(2, 2))
    e["eig2"] = max(e["eig2"], np.max(np.abs(np.sort_complex(eig2(A)) - np.sort_complex(np.linalg.eigvals(A).astype(complex)))))
for _ in range(200):
    n = int(rng.integers(2, 9)); S = simetrica_separada(n)
    w, V = np.linalg.eigh(S); i = np.argmax(np.abs(w))
    lam, v, _ = potencia(S, rng.normal(size=n), tol=1e-15, max_iter=200_000)
    e["pot"] = max(e["pot"], abs(lam - w[i]) / abs(w[i])); e["potv"] = max(e["potv"], mismo_vector(v, V[:, i]))
    j = rng.integers(n); mu = w[j] + 0.1 * rng.uniform(-1, 1) * np.min(np.abs(np.delete(w, j) - w[j]))
    li, vi, _ = potencia_inversa(S, mu)
    e["inv"] = max(e["inv"], abs(li - w[j]) / np.max(np.abs(w)))
    ld, Vd = deflacion(S)
    e["def"] = max(e["def"], np.max(np.abs(np.sort(ld) - w)) / np.max(np.abs(w)))
    lj, Vj = jacobi(S); lq, Vq, _ = qr_simetrica(S); ws, Vs = w[::-1], V[:, ::-1]
    e["jac"] = max(e["jac"], np.max(np.abs(lj - ws)) / np.max(np.abs(w)))
    e["jacv"] = max(e["jacv"], max(mismo_vector(Vj[:, k], Vs[:, k]) for k in range(n)))
    e["qr"] = max(e["qr"], np.max(np.abs(lq - ws)) / np.max(np.abs(w)))
    e["qrv"] = max(e["qrv"], max(mismo_vector(Vq[:, k], Vs[:, k]) for k in range(n)))
    e["rec"] = max(e["rec"], np.max(np.abs(Vj @ np.diag(lj) @ Vj.T - S)) / np.max(np.abs(S)),
                   np.max(np.abs(Vj.T @ Vj - np.eye(n))))
for _ in range(200):
    n = int(rng.integers(2, 8)); P = rng.uniform(0, 1, (n, n)) ** 2 + 0.01; P /= P.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    w, VL = np.linalg.eig(P.T); k = np.argmin(np.abs(w - 1)); ref = np.real(VL[:, k]); ref /= ref.sum()
    e["est"] = max(e["est"], np.max(np.abs(estacionaria(P) - ref)), np.max(np.abs(estacionaria(P, "lineal") - ref)))
for _ in range(100):
    n, p = int(rng.integers(20, 200)), int(rng.integers(2, 7))
    X = rng.normal(size=(n, p)) @ rng.normal(size=(p, p)) + rng.normal(size=p) * 5
    comp, var, mu = pca(X); sk = PCA().fit(X)
    e["pca"] = max(e["pca"], np.max(np.abs(var - sk.explained_variance_)) / var[0])
    e["pcav"] = max(e["pcav"], max(mismo_vector(comp[k], sk.components_[k]) for k in range(p)))
    e["evr"] = max(e["evr"], np.max(np.abs(var / var.sum() - sk.explained_variance_ratio_)))

print(f"eig2 (trace and determinant) vs np.linalg.eigvals, 300 2×2 matrices  {e['eig2']:.1e}")
print(f"potencia: dominant λ vs eigh (relative)                              {e['pot']:.1e}")
print(f"potencia: eigenvector vs eigh (up to sign)                           {e['potv']:.1e}")
print(f"potencia_inversa (shifted): λ closest to μ                           {e['inv']:.1e}")
print(f"deflacion (all λ) vs eigh                                            {e['def']:.1e}")
print(f"jacobi: λ vs eigh | eigenvectors (up to sign)                        {e['jac']:.1e} | {e['jacv']:.1e}")
print(f"qr_simetrica: λ vs eigh | eigenvectors (up to sign)                  {e['qr']:.1e} | {e['qrv']:.1e}")
print(f"V diag(λ) Vᵀ − S and VᵀV − I (Jacobi)                                {e['rec']:.1e}")
print(f"estacionaria (power and linear) vs eigenvector of Pᵀ with λ = 1      {e['est']:.1e}")
print(f"pca: variances vs sklearn explained_variance_ (relative)             {e['pca']:.1e}")
print(f"pca: components vs sklearn components_ (up to sign)                  {e['pcav']:.1e}")
print(f"pca: explained ratio vs explained_variance_ratio_                    {e['evr']:.1e}")

Eigenvectors are compared with mismo_vector, which takes the minimum of and : NumPy, scikit-learn and Jacobi can return each eigenvector with the opposite sign, and both answers are correct (scikit-learn fixes the sign with its own rule, svd_flip; here pca fixes another). Jacobi and QR reach machine rounding. The interesting one is the power method: the eigenvalue has error and the eigenvector, . It's not a bug: the stopping criterion requires , and with an eigenvector correct to the Rayleigh quotient is already correct to (quadratic error, §3). Deflation accumulates error from one pair to the next () and costs power runs: it is only useful for a few dominant eigenvalues.

§8 · In the fleet

Estimated state table, stationary distribution, mixing and PCA of telemetry

200 trucks over 180 days with the three-state chain of the simple version (on the road, in the shop, idle). The analyst doesn't know : they estimate it by counting changes, and from it they get how much of the fleet will be available and how long it takes to recover. Then, PCA of five signals from 600 trips that depend on two hidden causes: the load and the type of road.

flota.py

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from autovectores import estacionaria, tiempo_mezcla, pca

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
ESTADOS = ["on the road", "in the shop", "idle"]
P = np.array([[0.90, 0.03, 0.07],
              [0.30, 0.60, 0.10],
              [0.50, 0.02, 0.48]])                 # the “true” table, unknown to the analyst

# 1) simulate 200 trucks over 180 days and estimate the table by counting changes
n_cam, n_dias = 200, 180
est = np.zeros((n_cam, n_dias), int); est[:, 0] = rng.choice(3, n_cam)
for t in range(1, n_dias):
    u = rng.random(n_cam)[:, None]
    est[:, t] = (u > np.cumsum(P[est[:, t - 1]], axis=1)).sum(1)
C = np.zeros((3, 3))
np.add.at(C, (est[:, :-1].ravel(), est[:, 1:].ravel()), 1)
Ph = C / C.sum(1, keepdims=True)
print("transitions counted:", int(C.sum()))
print("estimated P:\n", Ph.round(3))
pi_h = estacionaria(Ph); pi = estacionaria(P, "lineal")
ocup = np.bincount(est[:, 30:].ravel(), minlength=3) / est[:, 30:].size
print("estimated stationary  ", pi_h.round(4), "  true", pi.round(4), "  observed occupancy (days 30+)", ocup.round(4))
w = np.sort(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(Ph.T)))[::-1]
print("|eigenvalues| of estimated P", w.round(4), "  half-life of a deviation:", round(np.log(2) / -np.log(w[1]), 2), "days")
print("mixing time (TV < 1%):", tiempo_mezcla(Ph), "days   (with the true P:", tiempo_mezcla(P), ")")
print("expected days in the shop per visit, 1/(1 − P̂[1, 1]):", round(1 / (1 - Ph[1, 1]), 2), " mean return time to the shop 1/π:", round(1 / pi_h[1], 1), "days")

# 2) what if the shop takes longer? (the diagonal 0.60 → 0.80)
P2 = P.copy(); P2[1] = [0.15, 0.80, 0.05]
pi2 = estacionaria(P2, "lineal"); w2 = np.sort(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(P2.T)))[::-1]
print("slow shop: stationary", pi2.round(4), " trucks on the road out of 200:", round(200 * pi2[0], 1),
      " |λ₂| =", round(w2[1], 4), " mixing:", tiempo_mezcla(P2), "days")

# 3) telemetry PCA: 600 trips, 5 signals that depend on 2 causes (load and road type)
n = 600; carga = rng.uniform(0, 1, n); via = rng.uniform(0, 1, n)        # 0 = city, 1 = highway
X = np.c_[45 + 40 * via + rng.normal(0, 4, n),                           # average speed (km/h)
          1500 - 300 * via + 250 * carga + rng.normal(0, 60, n),         # average rpm
          24 + 12 * carga - 4 * via + rng.normal(0, 1.2, n),             # fuel use (L/100 km)
          88 + 6 * carga + rng.normal(0, 1.0, n),                        # engine temperature (°C)
          95 + 7 * carga + 0.5 * rng.normal(0, 1.0, n) + rng.normal(0, 1.0, n)]   # oil temperature (°C)
Z = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0, ddof=1)                                   # without standardizing, rpm would dominate
comp, var, _ = pca(Z); sk = PCA().fit(Z)
print("explained variance (from scratch):", (var / var.sum()).round(4))
print("explained variance (sklearn):     ", sk.explained_variance_ratio_.round(4))
print("component 1:", comp[0].round(3), "\ncomponent 2:", comp[1].round(3))
print("correlation of component 1 with load:", round(abs(np.corrcoef(Z @ comp[0], carga)[0, 1]), 3),
      "  of 2 with road type:", round(abs(np.corrcoef(Z @ comp[1], via)[0, 1]), 3))

# estimated P:
#  [[0.901 0.029 0.07 ]
#  [0.294 0.61  0.096]
#  [0.499 0.022 0.479]]
# estimated stationary   [0.8107 0.0678 0.1215]   true [0.811  0.0669 0.122 ]   observed occupancy (days 30+) [0.8106 0.0675 0.1219]
# |eigenvalues| of estimated P [1.     0.5791 0.41  ]   half-life of a deviation: 1.27 days
# mixing time (TV < 1%): 9 days   (with the true P: 9 )
# expected days in the shop per visit, 1/(1 − P̂[1, 1]): 2.56  mean return time to the shop 1/π: 14.8 days
# slow shop: stationary [0.7601 0.1255 0.1144]  trucks on the road out of 200: 152.0  |λ₂| = 0.7706  mixing: 18 days
# explained variance (from scratch): [0.6166 0.2703 0.0496 0.0379 0.0256]
# explained variance (sklearn):      [0.6166 0.2703 0.0496 0.0379 0.0256]
# component 1: [-0.184  0.459  0.542  0.48   0.481]

With 35,800 transitions, is off by at most 0.01 per cell, and the estimated stationary distribution (81.1% on the road, 6.8% in the shop, 12.2% idle) differs from the true one and from the observed occupancy by less than a tenth of a point: with 200 trucks, about 162 available and 13 in the shop on any given day. means that a deviation (a spike in breakdowns) is halved in 1.3 days and that within 9 days the fleet has completely forgotten its initial state. If the shop becomes slow (staying probability 0.80 instead of 0.60), it's not just that trucks on the road drop from 162 to 152: rises to 0.77 and the mixing time doubles, to 18 days. Both figures come from the same matrix, from its first and second eigenvectors.

In the PCA, without standardizing, the rpm (with a standard deviation in the hundreds) would take the first component on their own; standardized, two components explain 88.7% of the variance of five signals and each one correlates 0.89 with one cause: component 1 weighs fuel use, temperatures and rpm (the load), and component 2 mostly speed, against rpm (city or highway). The remaining three, with 11%, are sensor noise. pca from scratch and sklearn.decomposition.PCA give the same ratios.

§9 · Checklist

Before you trust some eigenvalues

  • Is it symmetric? Use eigh, not eig: faster, real eigenvalues sorted (from smallest to largest) and orthonormal vectors. Symmetrize with if rounding has broken it.
  • Never compare eigenvectors with ==: the sign (and, with repeated eigenvalues, the whole basis of the subspace) is arbitrary. Fix a sign convention if you are going to display them or compare them across runs.
  • With eig, eigenvalues can come out complex even when you expect real ones (imaginary part of ): take .real only after checking that the imaginary part is negligible.
  • Don't compute or by diagonalizing an ill-conditioned non-symmetric matrix: look at or use Schur or matrix_power.
  • For a few eigenvalues of a large or sparse matrix, eigsh/eigs; never eig on a dense .
  • Markov: check that the rows add up to 1, that the chain is irreducible and aperiodic, and normalize the eigenvector so it adds up to 1 (and has no negative sign).
  • Stability of an iterated system: look at , but if is highly non-normal also check (transient growth).
  • PCA: center, decide whether to standardize (different units: yes) and compute via SVD.

§10 · Worked example

A symmetric matrix and a truck that goes to the shop

The characteristic polynomial, the eigenvalues, the eigenvectors, the powers and a stationary distribution, by hand and with the numbers of the simple version.

The setup. The fleet analyst wants to understand two small matrices before trusting what numpy returns: the one behind the toy's “symmetric” button, which is also the one in idea 2, and the two-state table of idea 3 (a truck that goes in and out of the maintenance shop). Everything fits on one sheet.

Example map

The “symmetric” matrix of the toy in the simple version and the two-state chain of its idea 3. We compute by hand the characteristic polynomial, the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors; we check that the matrix only stretches them; we use diagonalization to compute a power without multiplying and to explain the power method of idea 2; and we get the stationary distribution of a truck that goes in and out of the maintenance shop, with its speed of convergence.

  1. The characteristic polynomial.
  2. The eigenvalues.
  3. The eigenvectors, and the check .
  4. Powers and the power method.
  5. A truck between the road and the shop: the stationary distribution.
  6. How long it takes to forget the starting day.

  1. The characteristic polynomial

    In words

    We look for numbers for which there is an arrow with . Moving everything to one side, : the matrix has to squash an arrow that is not zero, and that only happens if its determinant (its area factor, topic 3) is 0.

    The math

    Where does each number come from?

    The 2s on the diagonal and the 1s off it are the matrix of the “symmetric” button in the simple version: the arrow → ends up at (2, 1) and ↑ at (1, 2). is the identity, and subtracting only subtracts from the diagonal. For a 2 × 2 the polynomial is always : here (the trace, the sum of the diagonal) and (the determinant).

    What it means: the eigenvalues are the roots of . We already know two things without solving anything: they add up to 4 (the trace) and multiply to 3 (the determinant).

  2. The eigenvalues

    The math

    What if it were the root of a negative number?

    The number under the root, , is the discriminant. If it were negative (for example, the 37° rotation of the simple version, with and : ), there would be no real eigenvalues: it's the “every arrow turns” case. In a symmetric matrix it never happens: .

    What it means: there is one direction that stretches × 3 and another that stays the same (× 1). They are the two big figures of the toy.

  3. The eigenvectors, and the check

    In words

    For each eigenvalue, we solve . Since the determinant is 0, the two equations say the same thing and one is enough.

    The math

    Why (1, 1) and not some other arrow?

    Any multiple works: (2, 2) or (−1, −1) also satisfy . What is determined is the direction (45° for , 135° for ). Libraries return the one of length 1, , with a sign that can vary. The dot product 0 (topic 2) confirms the right angle promised by the spectral theorem (§3).

    What it means: they are the dashed lines of the toy, at 45° and 135°. In the basis , the matrix only multiplies the first coordinate by 3 and leaves the second one as is.

  4. Powers and the power method

    In words

    We write the starting arrow of idea 2, (1, 0), as a mix of the two eigendirections. Applying times multiplies the part by and the part by .

    The math

    kAk·(1, 0)angleleft to 45°Rayleigh
    0(1, 0)0°45°2
    1(2, 1)26.57°18.43°2.8
    2(5, 4)38.66°6.34°2.9756
    3(14, 13)42.88°2.12°2.9973
    4(41, 40)44.29°0.71°2.9997

    Where do the 1/2, the last column and the speed come from?

    The two are the coordinates of (1, 0) in the eigenbasis: . What's left to 45° is , because the purple part weighs relative to the orange one: each step divides it by . The “Rayleigh” column is the quotient , the estimate of given by the power method; its error, , drops like , twice as fast as the angle (§4). comes from the same formula applied to (1, 0) and (0, 1), without multiplying five matrices.

    What it means: these are the steps 26.6°, 38.7°, 42.9° and 44.3° of idea 2. The length grows × 3 per step because ; with the direction would converge just the same, but the length would fade out.

  5. A truck between the road and the shop: the stationary distribution

    In words

    With two states, a truck on the road today stays on the road tomorrow with probability 0.9 and goes into the shop with 0.1; one in the shop comes out with 0.6 and stays in with 0.4. We look for the split that the table leaves unchanged: .

    The math

    What is each number, and why does eigenvalue 1 come out?

    0.9 / 0.1out of every 10 trucks on the road, 9 stay on it and 1 goes into the shop the next day
    0.6 / 0.4out of every 10 in the shop, 6 come out the next day and 4 stay in
    0.6·πT = 0.1·πRin equilibrium, the trucks leaving the shop each day equal the ones going in
    1.3 and 0.3the trace of (0.9 + 0.4) and its determinant (0.9 · 0.4 − 0.1 · 0.6)

    These are example values from the simple version, not data from a real maintenance shop. Each row of adds up to 1 (the truck is somewhere), so : 1 is an eigenvalue of and therefore of (same polynomial). The stationary distribution is the eigenvector of for that 1, normalized to add up to 1. Check: .

    What it means: in the long run, a truck spends 85.7% of its days on the road and 14.3% in the shop; in a fleet of 70, about 10 are in the shop on any given day. Each visit lasts days on average.

  6. How long it takes to forget the starting day

    In words

    The split on any day is the stationary distribution plus a remainder along the direction of the other eigenvector. That remainder is multiplied by the second eigenvalue, 0.3, every day.

    The math (starting with the truck in the shop)

    Where do the subtracted 6/7 and the 0.3 come from?

    On day 0, , so the initial remainder is . The 0.3 is the second eigenvalue from the previous step: in a two-state chain with it is always , here . On day 1, 0.6 is exactly the probability of leaving the shop; on day 2, , as in idea 3.

    What it means: each day 30% of the difference remains; after 4 days less than 1% is left (). If the shop were slower (leaving with 0.2 instead of 0.6), the second eigenvalue would be 0.7 and it would take 13 days: the second eigenvalue measures the system's memory.

ejemplo.py · reproduces the numbers above

import numpy as np
from autovectores import eig2, potencia, estacionaria

A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
t, d = np.trace(A), np.linalg.det(A)
print("trace", t, " det", round(d, 10), " λ =", eig2(A))                         # λ² − 4λ + 3 = 0
v1, v2 = np.array([1, 1]) / np.sqrt(2), np.array([1, -1]) / np.sqrt(2)
print("A v1 =", (A @ v1 * np.sqrt(2)).round(12), "= 3·(1, 1)   A v2 =", (A @ v2 * np.sqrt(2)).round(12), "= 1·(1, −1)   v1·v2 =", round(v1 @ v2, 12) + 0.0)
Q = np.c_[v1, v2]; L = np.diag([3.0, 1.0])
print("Q Λ Qᵀ =", (Q @ L @ Q.T).round(12).tolist(), "  A⁵ =", np.linalg.matrix_power(A, 5).tolist(), "  (3⁵ ± 1)/2 =", (3**5 + 1) / 2, (3**5 - 1) / 2)
x = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
for k in range(5):
    print(" step", k, x, " angle", round(np.degrees(np.arctan2(x[1], x[0])), 2), "°  ‖Ax‖/‖x‖ =", round(np.linalg.norm(A @ x) / np.linalg.norm(x), 4),
          " Rayleigh xᵀAx/xᵀx =", round(x @ A @ x / (x @ x), 6))
    x = A @ x
lam, v, k = potencia(A, [1, 0]); print(f"potencia(): λ = {lam:.12f}, v = {v.round(6)}, {k} iterations")
P = np.array([[0.9, 0.1], [0.6, 0.4]])
print("stationary", estacionaria(P, "lineal"), " eigenvalues of Pᵀ", np.linalg.eigvals(P.T).real, " trace − 1 =", round(np.trace(P) - 1, 10))
p = np.array([0.0, 1.0])
for k in range(5):
    print(" day", k, p.round(4), " formula 6/7 − (6/7)·0.3^k =", round(6 / 7 - 6 / 7 * 0.3**k, 4)); p = p @ P

What would change in a real system

  • Large matrices: no characteristic polynomial; eigh for dense ones, eigsh for sparse ones.
  • Estimated table: comes from counting transitions, with error; it's best to give the stationary distribution with an interval (by resampling trucks).
  • More states: breakdowns by type, loading, at the border; the stationary distribution and are computed the same way.
  • Seasonality: if the table changes with the season, the chain is not homogeneous and the stationary distribution of an average table can mislead.
